lines.note: Hashitaka names a kind of hawk. The Portuguese gives only a broad falcon category, so a modern species identification is not supplied.
Hashitamono here means something incomplete or falling short. The scan reads Couſa, not Conta; the adjective imperfeita describes the thing, not necessarily an account.
The shortfall may concern a number or a piece of work. This continues the preceding definition and should not be read as a separate Japanese entry.
Hashitamono and hashita are alternative names for female servants in this entry, distinct from the numerical sense immediately above. The Portuguese molhe- continues below.

runs.text: res baixas que ſeruem em caſa dos ſenhores.

lines.note: The definition describes lower-ranking women serving in lords' households. Baixas is a social classification in the dictionary's wording, not a modern judgment added here.

runs.text: Couſa imperfeita, ou que não he in-

lines.note: Hashitana denotes something incomplete. The final in- belongs to inteira on the following line; it is not a separate abbreviated word.
This completes the description as not whole or complete in number. The qualification helps distinguish this entry from the harshness sense of hashitanai below.
Hashitanai is glossed as harsh or rough, rather than simply the modern sense 'immodest.' The following literary example is needed to understand that range.
Hashitanai kotogara ni naru is followed by a Feiq. citation, not more Japanese. The gloss below interprets the expression in terms of harsh speech.
The numeral completes the citation to book 2; the remaining words explain speaking harshly or showing harshness. Historical aſperamente is retained without modern accentuation.
Nas palauras completes 'show harshness in one's words.' This short Portuguese line belongs to the example above, not to the derivative below.
Hashitanasa is the nominal derivative in -sa, expressing harshness. Its isolated placement does not imply a missing Portuguese definition.
Hashitanǒ is the contracted adverbial form of hashitanai. The open long-vowel mark is preserved rather than replacing it with the modern -ku ending.
Hashiyagashi represents hashiyagasu, to dry something, here by heat. This is a drying sense of the hasyag- family, not the modern excited-behavior sense alone.
Ao fogo specifies drying at the fire. The whole short line qualifies the verb above; no additional Japanese text is implied.
Hashiyage is the related drying form; Idem refers back to the preceding definition. The historical stem and supplied inflection are retained rather than modernized.
Hashizume is the beginning or approach of a bridge. The spelling zz gives the historical voiced tsu-series sound, consistent with the compound's second member.
Hashǒ is explained by nami no ue, 'on the waves.' The scan abbreviates ondas as õdas; the Japanese long vowel belongs to the Sino-Japanese compound, not hashi 'bridge.'
Hassen appears in the calendrical expression doyǒ hassen. The Portuguese begins con- here and continues junções below; Vt introduces the Japanese example.

runs.text: junções, ou constellações de tempos q̃ concorrẽ

lines.note: Junções completes conjunções, describing calendrical conjunctions or combinations. The initial descender is j, not long s, and the visible nasal mark is retained.

runs.text: por vezes no anno, as quais os Iapões obſer-

lines.note: The periods recur during the year and are observed by Japanese people. This is the dictionary's account of calendrical practice, not an endorsement of its predictive validity.

runs.text: uão pera fazer algũa couſa, ou deixar de a

lines.note: The sentence says these times affect whether an activity is undertaken or omitted. Algũa keeps the scan's nasal abbreviation rather than spelling out alguma.
Fazer closes deixar de a fazer: to refrain from doing it. Its small physical row remains part of the full calendrical explanation.

runs.text: Hum pequeno de pao que ſe quei-

lines.note: Hassenmai names a small wooden piece burned ritually. The scan includes de before pao, despite the compressed phrase Hum pequeno de pao.

runs.text: ma diante do Idolo cõ certas cerimonias.

lines.note: The wooden piece is burned before an idol with ceremonies. Idolo is the missionary dictionary's terminology; the line does not establish a more precise ritual identification.

runs.text: Lei, ou prohibição: a propria palaura

lines.note: Hasseqi is glossed as a law or prohibition, then explicitly redirected to another form. The difference between e and i is intentional in the printed explanation.
The preferred form is Faxxiqi, hashiki. It is an embedded Japanese spelling in Portuguese prose, not a new definition or an error to harmonize with Faxxeqi.
Here hassuru means to expel or exclude. The Portuguese afastar/botar fora supports this sense, distinct from 'emit' in the next homographic entry.
Konnichi yori chōrui no ichimon wo supplies 'from today, from the family of birds.' The object belongs to the verb on the next physical line.
Hassuru zo to completes the quoted exclusion; Fab. is its source label. Deſdoje begins the Portuguese rendering 'from today we exclude you.'
This completes exclui-mos and identifies the family of birds, matching chōrui no ichimon. The cross-line syntax explains the otherwise abrupt initial fragment.
This second hassuru entry means to stir or bring forth. Its examples concern anger, words, and voice, rather than exclusion from a group.
Ikari wo hassuru means to give vent to anger. The next example switches from object-marker wo to subject-marker ga; the capital I is visible at the row's beginning.
The first hassuru finishes 'anger arises'; gongo wo hassuru then introduces uttering words. The shared verb has two differently structured examples on this line.
The Portuguese 'begin to speak' explains gongo wo hassuru. Koe wo hassuru introduces the separate example of emitting one's voice.
Deitar a voz gives the voice-emission sense, completing the previous example. It is not the start of the following legal entry.
Hashiki is glossed by hatto and nori, both law-related words. This confirms the earlier cross-reference from hasseqi without requiring identical Portuguese spelling of lei/Ley.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de dar a frecha, ou

lines.note: Hashitto is an expressive adverb for an arrow striking or a blow landing. The word frecha is historical Portuguese and is not normalized to flecha.
The scan reads pancada, a blow, not pancara. It completes the paired impact examples used to explain the Japanese expressive adverb.

runs.text: As oito ſeitas que ha em Iapão: ſ.

lines.note: Hasshū denotes eight Buddhist schools in Japan. The following list supplies the eight; the printed ù is retained although modern romanization would use ū.

runs.text: Faſſǒ, ſanron, cuxa, jǒjit, rixù, qe-

lines.note: The list begins Hossō, Sanron, Kusha, Jōjitsu, and Risshū, then qe- starts Kegon. The scan's rixù supports Risshū, not the earlier OCR nixù.
Gon completes qe-gon, followed by Tendai and Shingon. Together with the preceding row these are the eight schools, not four additional headwords.
Hasshun means eighty years, matching oitenta annos. Its final n distinguishes it from hasshū 'eight schools' immediately above.
Haya is an adverb 'already,' represented by Portuguese Ia. The i/j historical spelling is kept rather than silently changing it to modern já.
Hayabashiri is a courier and also the act of going rapidly. Item opens a second sense within the same entry, continued on the next row.
Correr de preſſa completes the rapid-motion sense of hayabashiri. It does not introduce another kind of courier.
Hayabaya is an adverb meaning quickly or early. The doubled Japanese element corresponds to the concise Portuguese de preſſa.
Hayabayashii describes something hurried. Final ij represents a long i sequence; it is not a consonantal j or an additional syllable.
Hayabayashisa is the -sa noun formed from the preceding adjective. Its physical line supplies a derivative, without a repeated Portuguese definition.
Hayabayashù is the contracted adverbial derivative. The grave-shaped mark over u is retained as printed rather than converted to a modern macron.
Hayabumi is a hurried or urgent letter. Carta contrasts it with hayabusa, the bird name immediately below, despite their similar beginnings.
Hayabusa names a kind of falcon. The definition is broad; no particular modern taxonomic species is inferred from it.
Hayakuchi here designates someone who speaks quickly. The Portuguese is personal, O que fala, rather than only the abstract act of rapid speech.
Hayakuchi ni is the adverbial form, repeated at the start of its example. The ni combines with the speech expression on the following line.
Mono wo yǔ completes 'speak rapidly.' The mark over u has two visible arms here; the kana guide's meaning should not depend on expanding it into modern iu.
Hayahaya is translated by the doubled instruction 'quickly, quickly.' The repeated Portuguese wording parallels the emphatic Japanese reduplication.
Hayafune means a fast vessel. Embarcação ligeira supports fune 'boat,' not a similarly shaped personal or place name.
Hayagaki denotes a scribe who writes rapidly in this definition. It is not only the act of rapid writing implied by the modern compound in isolation.
Hayai is glossed as hurried or swift. The two Portuguese adjectives give the basis for both derivative forms printed below.
Hayasa is the nominal derivative; hayǒ is the contracted adverbial form. Their side-by-side position preserves the dictionary's concise derivative notation.

runs.text: Mato pequeno, ou de poucas aruores.

lines.note: Hayama is a small or sparsely wooded area. The next line explicitly supplies its opposite, so a reading connected to haste is inappropriate here.
Shigeyama is the densely wooded counterpart to hayama. Xigueyama is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese sentence 'the opposite is.'
Hayamaru means for something to happen quickly or ahead of time. The final preſ- continues below; the definition is broader than a modern moral sense of acting rashly.

runs.text: ſa, ou ãtes do tẽpo determinado, ou anticiparſe

lines.note: The definition specifies before the appointed time or an event being advanced. The scan has the nasal abbreviation ãtes, not fully written antes.
A feast or invitation may take place earlier. No Cami introduces a regional equivalent; Cami belongs within the italic Portuguese explanation in this printing.
Torikosu is the regional alternative, 'bring forward' in this scheduling context. Its italic setting does not make it a Portuguese word.
Hayame gives the transitive verb 'hasten.' The supplied uru belongs to the older hayamuru paradigm, not an error to replace with modern hayameru.
Uma wo hayamuru means to make a horse go faster. The Portuguese causative fazer andar corresponds to the Japanese transitive construction.
The object o caualo closes the example's Portuguese gloss. This short row is essential to the horse example rather than an isolated definition.
Hayamichi is a courier and also travel by post. The second sense begins here and is completed by posta on the next row.
Hayamichi wo noru is illustrated as traveling by post. Nōru need not be supplied with an accent: the printed short noru is appropriate.
Hayarakasu is the causative 'make something circulate or become current.' The object is a custom or art, not a literal runner.
Cuſtume and arte complete the objects of fazer correr. This supports the spread-of-practice sense of the Japanese verb above.
Hayaru means for a custom or art to become current. It contrasts with the causative entry directly above and the impetuous-motion sense below.
Te completes ar-te. Despite its brevity, this row closes the cultural-practice definition before the next hayaru entry.

runs.text: Correr o rio com grande im-

lines.note: This hayaru entry describes a river rushing with force. The different sense is explicit in o rio, not inferred merely from the repeated headword.
Im-peto finishes the river definition, then Item introduces personal eagerness or impetuosity. Arrebata- continues on the next row.

runs.text: do como pera arremeter aos inimigos fora de

lines.note: The impetuous person may charge enemies too early. The military context supplies the sense of rash eagerness rather than fashionable popularity.
Tẽpo completes fora de tẽpo, 'at the wrong time.' Its nasal abbreviation is retained without expanding the missing m.
Hayariai describes mutually showing spirit or eagerness. The supplied ǒ is the contracted ending for hayariau, as also represented in the headword index.
The participants fight one another with spirit and fervor. Entre ſi supplies the reciprocal relationship expressed by Japanese -ai.
Hayarimono or hayattamono names an eager, spirited soldier. The Portuguese a- begins animoso below rather than constituting a complete article.

runs.text: nimoſo, & forte, & que acomete dos pri-

lines.note: The soldier is spirited, strong, and among the first to attack. The final pri- continues primeiros, which completes that comparison.
Meiros completes primeiros: one of the first. It remains attached to the soldier definition despite occupying its own physical row.
Hayate is a sudden strong gust. The example repeats hayate here, with its case particle and verb placed on the next row.

runs.text: Encontrar com eſta refega, ou pè

lines.note: The scan reads ni vǒ, not mivǒ: hayate ni au means to encounter a gust. Portuguese encontrar confirms this interpretation; the printed contracted vǒ is retained.
De vento completes pè de vento, another expression for a gust. This is still the hayate example's translation.
Hayawaza describes quick work or dexterity. The Portuguese coordinates ligeireza with the following row's manual skill.
Deſtreza de mãos specifies dexterity of the hands. This is a continuation of the compound's explanation, not a second headword.
Hayauchi is glossed simply as a courier. It belongs to the rapid-message family around hayabumi, hayamichi, and hayauma.
Hayauma is a swift horse; the example separates faya vma wo in print. That word spacing is retained rather than forced to match the headword.
Tatsuru or yaru completes dispatching a fast horse, rendered 'send by post.' The alternative-marker l is not part of either Japanese verb.

runs.text: Canauial, ou lugar de muitas aruores

lines.note: Hayashi names a cane thicket or a place with many trees. Canauial is read as the historical Portuguese form for a cane stand.
Juntas como boſque completes the definition: trees together like a wood. This is the end of the column's body, separate from the catchword.
